main.title: Final Fantasy XI
main.summary: Final Fantasy XI, also known as Final Fantasy XI Online, is a massively multiplayer online role-playing game (MMORPG), originally developed and published by Square and then published by Square Enix as the eleventh main installment of the Final Fantasy series.

cards.text: Final Fantasy XI, also known as Final Fantasy XI Online, is a massively multiplayer online role-playing game (MMORPG), originally developed and published by Square and then published by Square Enix as the eleventh main installment of the Final Fantasy series. Designed and produced by Hiromichi Tanaka, it was released in Japan on May 16, 2002, for PlayStation 2 and Microsoft Windows-based personal computers in November of that year. The game was the first MMORPG to offer cross-platform play between PlayStation 2 and Windows. It was later released for the Xbox 360 in April 2006. All versions of the game require a monthly subscription to play.

The story is set in the fantasy world of Vana'diel, where player-created avatars can both compete and cooperate in a variety of objectives to develop a range of jobs and skills, and earn in-game item rewards. Players can undertake an array of quests and progress through the in-game hierarchy and through the major plot of the game. Since its debut in 2002, five expansion packs have been released along with eight add-on scenarios. Each expansion pack and add-on brings a new major storyline to the Final Fantasy XI world, along with numerous areas, quests, events and item rewards.

In 2015, Square Enix released the final main scenario for Final Fantasy XI, titled Rhapsodies of Vana'diel. Final Fantasy XI became the final active server on the PlayStation 2 online service. Support for the PlayStation 2 and Xbox 360 versions ended on March 31, 2016, leaving only the PC platform playable. A mobile client for the game was under development by Square Enix in collaboration with Korean developer Nexon, using Unreal Engine 4, but was cancelled in late 2020. A spin-off mobile game, Final Fantasy Grandmasters was released on September 30, 2015. A new, episodic story series titled The Voracious Resurgence was added to the game in 2020. In May 2022 rumors circulated that FFXI might soon shut down, but Yoji Fujito released a statement noting that this was not the case and users should not worry about the services being shut down any time soon.

In 2025, a surge in new players, roughly coinciding with the release of the Echoes of Vana'diel raids within Final Fantasy XIV: Dawntrail, has resulted in overpopulation in several game servers ("worlds"). As a result, the server Asura was closed off for new characters on July 29, 2025, followed by Bahamut on October 9, 2025, Odin on March 10, 2026, and Phoenix on June 10, 2026. As of June 2026, those servers remain closed off. New characters cannot be created on these servers, except for secondary characters on accounts that already have a character on the same server, and existing characters cannot be transferred to those servers using the world transfer service.

main.title: Castlevania: Harmony of Dissonance
main.subtitle: A Belmont searches for a missing friend
main.summary: Castlevania: Harmony of Dissonance is Konami's second Game Boy Advance exploration adventure in the series. Juste Belmont, Simon's grandson, enters a mysterious castle while searching for his kidnapped childhood friend. His whip supplies the familiar starting point, while experience, equipment and magic develop his options as the journey continues. The castle's interconnected routes make movement abilities and remembered obstacles central to progress. What initially appears to be a single building becomes a more complicated place to understand, requiring attention to the relationship between its different versions as well as its individual rooms.

cards.text: Castlevania: Harmony of Dissonance is Konami's second Game Boy Advance exploration adventure in the series. Juste Belmont, Simon's grandson, enters a mysterious castle while searching for his kidnapped childhood friend. His whip supplies the familiar starting point, while experience, equipment and magic develop his options as the journey continues. The castle's interconnected routes make movement abilities and remembered obstacles central to progress. What initially appears to be a single building becomes a more complicated place to understand, requiring attention to the relationship between its different versions as well as its individual rooms.

cards.heading: A spell book changes a familiar subweapon
cards.text: Juste's magical options combine spell books with the subweapons found during exploration. The result depends on the pairing, allowing a familiar item to behave differently when another book is selected. This makes the growing collection useful through combinations rather than simply replacing an earlier attack with a stronger one. Whip combat remains available alongside those effects, giving the player several ways to approach a difficult enemy. Finding another magical component can therefore change the practical value of something already carried and invite another experiment before the next encounter begins.

cards.heading: Two versions of the same place
cards.text: Progress involves traversing two forms of the castle, with their maps creating related spaces that must be understood together. An ability or discovery in one part of the journey can open another route through the larger structure. Equipment and character growth support the same exploration, helping Juste survive the enemies guarding what remains unknown. Harmony of Dissonance uses the doubled setting to give the map a further layer of uncertainty, asking the player to recognise a place while still considering what may be different about its present form and available connections.

main.title: Phantom Crash
main.subtitle: Old Tokyo hosts a mechanical combat sport
main.summary: Phantom Crash is Genki's Xbox vehicular combat game, first released in Japan on 20 June 2002. In 2031, the abandoned streets of Old Tokyo have become arenas for a televised sport called Rumbling. The player arrives as an unknown competitor and attempts to climb its rankings in a customisable Scoot Vehicle. Winning a fight produces money for repairs and new parts, connecting success in the arena to the machine used in the next event. Conversations and shop visits place that mechanical career within a small community of rival pilots.

cards.text: Phantom Crash is Genki's Xbox vehicular combat game, first released in Japan on 20 June 2002. In 2031, the abandoned streets of Old Tokyo have become arenas for a televised sport called Rumbling. The player arrives as an unknown competitor and attempts to climb its rankings in a customisable Scoot Vehicle. Winning a fight produces money for repairs and new parts, connecting success in the arena to the machine used in the next event. Conversations and shop visits place that mechanical career within a small community of rival pilots.

cards.heading: Build for the weight limit and the way you move
cards.text: Arms, shoulders, legs and bodies can be changed, allowing the player to combine different weapons and handling characteristics. Event weight limits make equipment a choice rather than a list of upgrades to install indiscriminately. Optical camouflage briefly hides the vehicle, while rocket-assisted jumps add another way to cross the arena or escape an attack. Damage carries repair costs, so surviving efficiently matters alongside defeating competitors. A successful configuration needs to suit the player's movement and the restrictions of the event, turning the garage into a practical extension of each fight.

cards.heading: A daily routine around the arena
cards.text: Quest Mode advances through a day-to-day structure, with an event, shopping and story encounters reached through a map. Class captains provide milestones as the player works through the competitive ranks. Custom paint and the vehicle's personality-giving CHIPs add expression to the mechanical choices, while the soundtrack gives Rumbling a contemporary urban character. Reviews responded to the detailed machines and customisation, though the limited arenas and extensive dialogue divided opinion. Genki later revisited the idea in S.L.A.I., carrying the relationship between pilots, configurable machines and televised combat onto PlayStation 2.

main.title: Eternal Darkness: Sanity’s Requiem
main.subtitle: Horror across centuries
main.summary: Eternal Darkness: Sanity’s Requiem is a GameCube horror adventure that follows different people through a story spanning two millennia. Silicon Knights uses changing periods and locations to give an ancient struggle a human scale. Each chapter offers another perspective, with weapons and surroundings appropriate to its protagonist. Exploration, combat and rune-based magic connect these episodes. Alongside the danger inside the fiction, the game develops another source of unease: the possibility that the screen and interface themselves can no longer be completely trusted.

cards.heading: Horror across centuries
cards.text: Eternal Darkness: Sanity’s Requiem is a GameCube horror adventure that follows different people through a story spanning two millennia. Silicon Knights uses changing periods and locations to give an ancient struggle a human scale. Each chapter offers another perspective, with weapons and surroundings appropriate to its protagonist. Exploration, combat and rune-based magic connect these episodes. Alongside the danger inside the fiction, the game develops another source of unease: the possibility that the screen and interface themselves can no longer be completely trusted.

cards.heading: When sanity gives way
cards.text: The sanity meter falls when a character is seen by certain enemies. As it declines, the game introduces effects that disturb perception: a room may appear wrong, voices may intrude or an apparent technical problem may interrupt play. These moments turn the player’s familiarity with games into something the horror can exploit. Restoring sanity becomes a practical concern, supported by finishing enemies and using appropriate resources. The system gives being observed a consequence that reaches beyond the damage an enemy can inflict.

cards.heading: A body, a weapon, a rune
cards.text: Combat allows attacks on individual body parts, making the choice of target useful. Removing an enemy’s head changes how it can pursue the protagonist, while the available weapons vary with the historical setting. Magic offers another set of solutions through combinations of runes. It can support fighting and recovery or help reveal a way through an obstruction. These deliberate actions balance the more unpredictable sanity effects: the player must still read the room, choose a method and manage resources while the presentation encourages doubt.

main.title: Stuntman
main.summary: Stuntman is the name of two action-adventure racing video games; one was developed by Reflections Interactive for the PlayStation 2, and the other by Velez & Dubail for the Game Boy Advance, with both being published by Infogrames under the Atari brand name.

cards.text: Stuntman is the name of two action-adventure racing video games; one was developed by Reflections Interactive for the PlayStation 2, and the other by Velez & Dubail for the Game Boy Advance, with both being published by Infogrames under the Atari brand name. The games focus around the career of a motion-picture stuntman. It takes the player through various movies in which they perform dangerous stunts as called by the game.

Critical reaction to Stuntman varied. The game was hailed for its innovative gameplay and physics, but was criticised for being linear and its difficulty level requiring too many retries of levels. The game was the first installment in the Stuntman series, and was followed by Stuntman: Ignition (2007) and Stuntman: Hollywood (TBA).

main.title: Golden Sun: The Lost Age
main.subtitle: The journey continues from another side
main.summary: Golden Sun: The Lost Age is Camelot's Game Boy Advance role-playing sequel following Felix and his companions in their attempt to restore alchemy to Weyard. Taking characters associated with the opposing side of the first adventure gives the continuing journey another perspective. Psynergy again supplies both battle abilities and tools for environmental puzzles, while a wider structure allows more freedom in the order of several objectives. The sequel turns an unfinished story into another expedition, asking the player to reconsider its larger purpose while exploring more of the same elemental world.

cards.heading: Remember the place that still needs a power
cards.text: Exploration places more emphasis on returning to locations when another ability or discovery makes further progress possible. Psynergy continues to connect the party with its surroundings, allowing a newly available power to change what an earlier scene permits. The player develops a practical memory of unfinished routes as well as the map of places already visited. This makes the wider journey more than a succession of new destinations. A return can be the important next step once the group finally possesses the means of solving a problem that previously stopped its exploration.

cards.heading: The first adventure can travel with the second
cards.text: A password system or Game Link Cable can transfer information from the first Golden Sun, preserving aspects of the earlier party and its discoveries within the continuing story. The connection rewards treating the two cartridges as parts of one larger adventure. Djinn collection, turn-based battles and character preparation remain central as Felix's group develops its capabilities. The Lost Age gives those familiar systems another setting and perspective, allowing the accumulated knowledge of how elemental powers work to support a journey whose goals must still be understood through the characters now leading it.

main.title: Warcraft III: Reign of Chaos
main.summary: Warcraft III: Reign of Chaos is a high fantasy real-time strategy computer video game developed and published by Blizzard Entertainment released in July 2002.

cards.heading: Warcraft III: Reign of Chaos
cards.text: Warcraft III: Reign of Chaos is a high fantasy real-time strategy computer video game developed and published by Blizzard Entertainment released in July 2002. It is the second sequel to Warcraft: Orcs & Humans, after Warcraft II: Tides of Darkness, the third game set in the Warcraft fictional universe, and the first to be rendered in three dimensions. An expansion pack, The Frozen Throne, was released in July 2003. Warcraft III is set several years after the events of Warcraft II, and tells the story of the Burning Legion's attempt to conquer the fictional world of Azeroth with the help of an army of the Undead known as the Scourge, led by the fallen paladin Arthas Menethil. It chronicles the combined efforts of the Human Alliance, Orcish Horde, and Night Elves to stop them before they can corrupt the World Tree.

cards.heading: Four factions and hero units
cards.text: In the game, as in many real-time strategy (RTS) games, players collect resources, train individual units and heroes, and build bases in order to achieve various goals (in single-player mode), or to defeat the enemy player. Four playable factions can be chosen from: Humans, Orcs, (both of which appeared in the previous games) and two new factions: the Night Elves and the Undead. Warcraft III's single-player campaign is laid out similarly to that of StarCraft, and is told through the races in a progressive manner. Players can also play matches against the computer, or against others—using local area networking (LAN) or Blizzard's Battle.net gaming platform.

cards.heading: The project changes during development
cards.text: After Warcraft II: Beyond the Dark Portal, the last in the Warcraft saga, was released in 1996, Blizzard began development of a point-and-click adventure game called Warcraft Adventures: Lord of the Clans, which was supposed to continue the story. Lord of the Clans was canceled in favor of Warcraft III in 1998, which was presented to the public at the European Computer Trade Show in September 1999. The design changed substantially during development, leaving the final game quite different from the version first presented.

cards.heading: Reception and legacy
cards.text: The game received acclaim from critics, who praised the game's presentation and multiplayer features. It is considered an influential example of RTS video games and one of the greatest video games ever made. Warcraft III was a commercial success, shipping 4.4 million copies to retail stores, selling over a million within a month. Video game modifications created with the World Editor, such as Defense of the Ancients, led to lasting changes and inspired many future games. In 2020, Blizzard released a remastered version of both Warcraft III and its expansion, The Frozen Throne, called Warcraft III: Reforged.

main.title: America's Army: Operations
main.subtitle: A tactical shooter built for recruitment
main.summary: On July 4, 2002 the United States Army released America's Army: Operations, a free tactical shooter developed as a communication and recruiting tool.

cards.heading: A tactical shooter built for recruitment
cards.text: On July 4, 2002, the United States Army released America's Army: Operations, a free tactical shooter built as a communication and recruitment tool. Training, procedures, hierarchy and cooperation shape its representation of military life. Released on Independence Day, it linked playable combat directly to a real institution's efforts to reach potential recruits.

cards.heading: From an Army proposal to a development studio
cards.text: America's Army's concept was conceived in 1999 by Colonel Casey Wardynski, the Army's chief economist and a professor at the United States Military Academy. Wardynski envisioned "using computer game technology to provide the public a virtual soldier experience that was engaging, informative and entertaining". America's Army was managed by two other U.S. Army officers serving with Wardynski at the Office of Economic and Manpower Analysis (OEMA): Major Chris Chambers and Major Brett Wilson. Wardynski approached Michael Zyda and Michael Capps at the Naval Postgraduate School's (NPS) MOVES Institute in Monterey, California, to make this video game vision a reality. Zyda and Capps took a unique approach for developing a major software project in the United States Department of Defense by assembling a team of professional game developers with experience developing major titles and creating a development studio on the campus of NPS. The project had a development budget of $5 million.

cards.heading: Realism and its limitations
cards.text: Its detailed visual and acoustic representation of weapons and combat supported the Army's claim to authenticity. Critics questioned how accurately those playable encounters could convey wartime conditions. That debate accompanied its role as a recruitment project: the model of military life offered to players also served the institution that financed it.

cards.heading: Optional medical training and reported real-life use
cards.text: America's Army includes optional medical training designed to provide real-world information. In order to assume the role of combat lifesaver in the game, players must pass a virtual medical training course based on actual training that soldiers receive with regard to evaluating and prioritizing casualties, controlling bleeding, recognizing and treating shock, and administering aid when victims are not breathing. Two America's Army players have reported using the training they received in-game to save lives in emergency situations; one such account, by Paxton Galvanek, received national media attention.

main.title: Suikoden III
main.subtitle: A conflict seen from three sides
main.summary: Suikoden III is Konami's PlayStation 2 role-playing game, first released in Japan on 11 July 2002. Its story follows three protagonists connected to the tensions between the Grasslands, Zexen and Harmonia. Hugo belongs to a Grassland clan, Chris Lightfellow commands Zexen knights and Geddoe serves with a Harmonian frontier force. Moving between them gives the same conflict different meanings. The player learns about the people on each side before their paths converge, making the growth of a shared cause depend on understanding how those separate journeys began.

cards.text: Suikoden III is Konami's PlayStation 2 role-playing game, first released in Japan on 11 July 2002. Its story follows three protagonists connected to the tensions between the Grasslands, Zexen and Harmonia. Hugo belongs to a Grassland clan, Chris Lightfellow commands Zexen knights and Geddoe serves with a Harmonian frontier force. Moving between them gives the same conflict different meanings. The player learns about the people on each side before their paths converge, making the growth of a shared cause depend on understanding how those separate journeys began.

cards.heading: Choose whose story to follow next
cards.text: The Trinity Sight System divides the opening story between its principal viewpoints. Events experienced with one character gain another context when encountered through somebody else, so knowledge grows across the separate chapters. The player also recruits the series' Stars of Destiny, bringing a large cast into the developing alliance. These companions make the wider conflict tangible through individual meetings and tasks. A political situation that first appears as opposing groups gradually becomes a network of people who may be persuaded to help, each with a place in the campaign.

cards.heading: A series changes its viewpoint
cards.text: Suikoden III brought the series onto PlayStation 2 with three-dimensional characters and environments. Yoshitaka Murayama and Keiichi Isobe directed the project, while Michiru Yamane, Takashi Yoshida and Masahiko Kimura supplied the music. Its multiple protagonists distinguish it from the single central hero of the earlier games, giving the player a less settled view of the war. The Japanese and North American editions arrived in 2002. The game's defining choice remains its structure: before asking different people to fight together, it allows the player to spend time within their separate worlds.

main.title: Riviera: The Promised Land
main.summary: Riviera: The Promised Land is a 2002 role-playing video game developed by Sting Entertainment.

cards.text: Riviera: The Promised Land is a 2002 role-playing video game developed by Sting Entertainment. It was originally released for WonderSwan Color as the first episode of the Dept. Heaven series of games. It was later ported to Nintendo's Game Boy Advance in 2004, which Atlus USA released in North America in 2005. An enhanced remake was released for the PlayStation Portable in November 2006, and was released in July 2007 in North America by Atlus USA. In July 2023, an HD remaster was announced for Microsoft Windows, Nintendo Switch, iOS and Android. The HD remaster released for Windows in July 2024.

The player takes the role of Ein, a Grim Angel, who must battle against demons as well as antagonistic Grim Angels to seal away the four entities of evil known as the Accursed. He is accompanied by four heroines—Fia, Lina, Serene and Cierra—as well as his cat-like familiar Rose. Riviera also contains dating sim elements, as the hero can achieve multiple endings with the supporting characters through decisions made throughout the game.
